cues.text: It's Friday, May the twelfth, 2017. You walk into a hospital in England… and every computer screen is red.
A message says your files are locked. Pay three hundred dollars in bitcoin, or lose everything.
And it's not just this hospital. It's happening in over a hundred countries. At the same time.
The person who stops it? A twenty-two year old, in his bedroom, on his week off.
With ten dollars and sixty-nine cents.
And three months later… the FBI arrests him.
This is the story of the accidental hero who stopped a global cyberattack… and the secret that caught up with him.
The attack was called WannaCry. And it was ransomware: software that locks up your files and holds them hostage.
But WannaCry was worse than normal ransomware. It didn't wait for you to click a bad link. It spread by itself, from computer to computer, like a cold in a crowded room.
It used a hacking tool reportedly built by America's National Security Agency, called EternalBlue. A month earlier, a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers had leaked it online.
Microsoft had already released a fix in March. But huge numbers of computers had never installed it. Some were so old, they weren't even supported anymore.
So WannaCry tore through them. More than two hundred thousand computers. Factories. Train stations. Phone companies.
And in Britain, it hit the National Health Service. About a third of hospital trusts were disrupted. Around nineteen thousand appointments were cancelled.
Meanwhile, in a small seaside town in England, a young man named Marcus Hutchins was on a week off.
He was twenty-two. He'd taught himself most of what he knew about computers. And his job was taking malware apart, to see how it worked.
He came back from lunch, saw the news, and got hold of a copy of WannaCry.
And inside, he noticed something strange. Before attacking, the malware tried to visit a weird web address. A long, random jumble of letters.
And nobody owned it.
Researchers sometimes buy addresses like that, to watch what the malware does. So Marcus bought it. For ten dollars and sixty-nine cents.
And then… the attack started to slow down.
Here's why. Before infecting a computer, WannaCry checked that address. If nobody answered, it attacked. But if someone answered…
…it switched itself off.
Think of a burglar who knocks before breaking in. If nobody's home, he goes in. If someone answers, he runs. Marcus had just answered the door. For every computer in the world.
He later said that, at first, it was an accident. He didn't know buying the address would stop it.
Another researcher, Darien Huss, spotted the same switch at almost the same time. New versions of WannaCry appeared later. But the biggest wave had been stopped.

Overnight, Marcus became the accidental hero. Newspapers hunted for his real name, and found it.
And the attackers? Very few victims paid. In the end, the ransom added up to only a little over a hundred thousand dollars.
Months later, the American and British governments said they believed North Korea was behind WannaCry.
For a while, Marcus was the most famous good hacker on the planet.
Then, in August 2017, he flew to Las Vegas for one of the world's biggest hacker conferences, DEF CON.
At the airport, on his way home… the FBI arrested him.
Not for WannaCry. For something from years earlier, when he was a teenager.
Prosecutors said that back then, he had helped create malware that stole online banking passwords. It was called Kronos.
The hero who helped stop one of the biggest cyberattacks in history… could now face years in an American prison.
In 2019, Marcus pleaded guilty to two charges. He said he regretted those mistakes, and that he'd spent years using his skills to protect people instead.
And in July 2019, a judge made a decision that surprised a lot of people.
No prison. Time already served, and one year of supervised release.
The judge pointed to how young he was back then, how he had turned his life around… and the fact that he had helped stop WannaCry.
Today, Marcus still works in cybersecurity, on the side of the defenders.
So here's my question. Should one good deed wipe out a bad past? Or should the past still count? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe, because next time, there's another hacker story you won't believe.
Ten dollars and sixty-nine cents. Probably the best money anyone ever spent.
